Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Notably, two LC participants had positive IgM levels to CMV and EBV (data not shown).

> LC participants had lower EQ-VAS than CC at 4 and 8 months (p= 0.002 and p= 0.039, respectively), with no difference at 24 months (Fig. 5c).

> When participants were classified by recovery status at later time points (18-24months) using an EQindex threshold of 0.9, unrecovered LC participants had lower EBV avidity than recovered controls longitudinally, with the clearest group contrasts at 4 (median 70, versus 82, p= 0.005) and 8 months (median 66.5, versus 89, p= 0.002) (Fig. 5g).

> Lower-avidity LC participants had lower EQ-VAS at 4 and 8 months, while EQ-index was lower at 4 months; avidity also discriminated between recovered controls and unrecovered LC participants in exploratory ROC analyses.

> Participants were followed for up to 24 months after infection, with clinical and biological assessments performed at prespecified visits.

> All participants provided written informed consent before study procedures.

> Most LC participants were enrolled from the community (39, 75.0%), whereas nearly all controls were community-enrolled (50, 94.3%).

> As previously described in the ADAPT cohort 12, participants were recruited during the initial wave of COVID-19 up to emergence of omicron variant BA.1/2, from hospital and community locations following mild/moderate severity of infection.

> Participants were considered to have poor health if their EQ-5D-5L score was below than the lower 95% confidence interval of the population values.

> It is anticipated that the normative general population values in South Australia are comparable to the normative general population values where the participants were located (i.e., neighbouring state of New South Wales).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Notably, two LC participants had positive IgM levels to CMV and EBV (data not shown).
LC participants had lower EQ-VAS than CC at 4 and 8 months (p= 0.002 and p= 0.039, respectively), with no difference at 24 months (Fig. 5c).

When participants were classified by recovery status at later time points (18-24months) using an EQindex threshold of 0.9, unrecovered LC participants had lower EBV avidity than recovered controls longitudinally, with the clearest group contrasts at 4 (median 70, versus 82, p= 0.005) and 8 months (median 66.5, versus 89, p= 0.002) (Fig. 5g).

Lower-avidity LC participants had lower EQ-VAS at 4 and 8 months, while EQ-index was lower at 4 months; avidity also discriminated between recovered controls and unrecovered LC participants in exploratory ROC analyses.
Participants were followed for up to 24 months after infection, with clinical and biological assessments performed at prespecified visits.
All participants provided written informed consent before study procedures.
Most LC participants were enrolled from the community (39, 75.0%), whereas nearly all controls were community-enrolled (50, 94.3%).

As previously described in the ADAPT cohort 12, participants were recruited during the initial wave of COVID-19 up to emergence of omicron variant BA.1/2, from hospital and community locations following mild/moderate severity of infection.
Participants were considered to have poor health if their EQ-5D-5L score was below than the lower 95% confidence interval of the population values.

It is anticipated that the normative general population values in South Australia are comparable to the normative general population values where the participants were located (i.e., neighbouring state of New South Wales).

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). reproducibility_check.checklist_section: We ran the paper's 7 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. **0 of 7 scripts ran to the end**: 5 stopped with an error, 1 could not run on our server, 1 was not run. | Script | Result | What happened | |---|---|---| | de_analysis.r | Stopped with an error | Error in eval(e, envir = env) : object 'obj' not found | | generate_scores.r | Stopped with an error | Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection | | make_seurat_object.r | Not run | R cannot read the script: it contains a syntax error. | | naive_cells_analysis.r | Stopped with an error | Error in readChar(con, 5L, useBytes = TRUE) : cannot open the connection | | plots_for_paper.r | Stopped with an error | Error in readChar(con, 5L, useBytes = TRUE) : cannot open the connection | | proportion_analysis.r | Could not run on our server | It needs the R package speckle, which we could not install. This is not an error in the script. | | seurat_object.r | Stopped with an error | Error in gzfile(file, "rb") : cannot open the connection | ### How to make your code run on another computer We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **Files are missing from your deposit.** - generate_scores.r reads interferon_stimulated_response_genes_2011. - naive_cells_analysis.r reads palette2.Rdata. - seurat_object.r reads combined_all_SCT.rds. The script stops at the line that reads the file. 1. Find the file on your computer. 2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it. 3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it. **A file may have been renamed.** - plots_for_paper.r reads metadata.Rdata; your deposit holds final_metadata.rdata. Check whether they are the same file. If so, use one name in both the script and the deposit. **A package could not be installed.** - proportion_analysis.r needs speckle. speckle could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version. **A script uses something it does not create or load itself.** - de_analysis.r: obj Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it. 1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R). 2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing. 3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second. 4. Load every package with library() at the top. **R or Python could not read a script, because of a mistake in the code itself.** - make_seurat_object.r Run each script once in a fresh session before you deposit it; the error message shows the line to fix. ### Other problems in the files - make_seurat_object.r calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.
